title: EPW Committee Announces Markup of the Water Resources Development Act of 2026
description:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the EPW Committee, announced plans for the EPW Committee to mark up the bipartisan Water Resources Development Act of 2026 (WRDA 2026) on Wednesday, July 15, 2026.
 

The Water Resources Development Act is biennial legislation that authorizes flood risk management, navigation, and ecosystem restoration projects for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Corps). WRDA 2026 also reauthorizes the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) drinking water and wastewater infrastructure programs, including the State Revolving Funds (SRFs). The legislation was developed in partnership with Senators Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.), Chairman of the of the EPW Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee; Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Ranking Member of the EPW Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee; and Adam Schiff (D.Calif.), Ranking Member of the EPW Fisheries, Water, and Wildlife Subcommittee.

 

“The Army Corps of Engineers conducts essential work to modernize water resources infrastructure, manage risk from floods and coastal storms, and improve navigation along our waterways and at Ports. This work protects lives and property, and bolsters our economy. As Chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, I am proud to have led this bipartisan effort in crafting WRDA 2026, which will provide the Army Corps with the resources it needs to continue its critical work nationwide. WRDA 2026 will also help provide West Virginia with vital funds to address our water infrastructure needs. This bill includes key wins for West Virginia and all fifty states. I hope to see it move forward with strong bipartisan support during Wednesday’s business meeting,” said Chairman Capito.

 

“Our markup to advance this significant package of legislation demonstrates a bipartisan commitment to maintaining and upgrading the nation’s water infrastructure. The Ocean State stands to benefit much from this bill, which supports investments in safe drinking water and wastewater systems as well as flood risk management, ecosystem restoration, and navigation,” said Ranking Member Whitehouse.

 

“Under both Republican and Democrat leadership, members of the Environment and Public Works Committee have worked together to pass a bipartisan Water Resources Development Act every two years through regular order. This year’s WRDA is a testament to the continued cooperation of the committee, especially the leadership of Chairman Capito and Ranking Member Whitehouse. The bill delivers wins for communities across North Dakota and the nation by authorizing critical water infrastructure programs, advancing efforts to streamline project delivery, and pursuing key regulatory reforms. I look forward to working with my colleagues to get this done,” said Senator Cramer.

 

“As Ranking Member of the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee, I am so proud of this bipartisan effort and the commitment we've had to advancing this critical legislation. I’m especially proud to have fought for provisions that deliver real results for Maryland — from increasing the federal cost share for the Cumberland flood risk management project to extending federal participation in the Assateague Island Shoreline Restoration and authorizing a funding increase for the Chesapeake Bay Oyster Recovery Program. We’re working together to modernize our infrastructure, protect our habitats, accomplish our environmental goals, and support communities across the country and Maryland. That is worth celebrating,” said Senator Alsobrooks. 

 

“Our bipartisan legislation will provide critical resources to address water supply, conservation and development, advance resilient water infrastructure, and deliver clean drinking water to millions of Americans. In California, these investments will lower rising water bills, provide necessary flood protection, and modernize aging infrastructure to ensure reliable access to safe drinking water,” said Senator Schiff.

title: Hashem - The EPA quietly approved three new ”forever chemical” pesticides to be used on American food supply.   The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has quietly fast-tracked the approval of three hazardous PFAS herbicides—trifludimoxazin, diflufenican, and epyrifenacil—for use on major food crops like wheat, oats, and citrus.   This controversial regulatory surge brings the total number of approved forever chemical pesticides to five in under two years, representing a dramatic shift in chemical registration. Alarmingly, trifludimoxazin was greenlit despite internal EPA assessments flagging 'suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential' and warnings that it breaks down into 12 highly persistent PFAS variants that can contaminate local water systems.  Health advocates argue that the EPA’s hands-off approach to chemical mixtures leaves consumers exposed to a toxic cocktail, failing to enforce critical safety protections that safeguard children and pregnant women.   While the Environmental Working Group (EWG) maintains that consumers should continue eating plenty of fresh produce, they stress that the current regulatory system is failing by routinely waiving critical immunotoxicity tests.   The mounting environmental and biological footprint of these persistent compounds has sparked urgent calls for the federal government to halt new registrations and implement comprehensive testing before these toxins further saturate the food supply.  source: Amarelo, M. Nixon first proposed the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency 9 July 1970. As boring and dry as that factoid might seem, it’s really important right now to understand what the EPA was… | John Pabon
description:
Nixon first proposed the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency 9 July 1970. As boring and dry as that factoid might seem, it’s really important right now to understand what the EPA was meant to do, its legacy, and why its future is so uncertain.

On paper, the EPA brought together many of the different departments looking at conservation, pollution, and the environment. It was a pretty tangled mess spanning the Interior Department, Health, Education, Welfare, and other places. Nixon wanted them all under one roof sitting within the Executive Branch. The EPA would formally start that December under the leadership of William Ruckelshaus, the man who famously quit rather than follow the orders of Nixon during the Watergate scandal.

Over its history, the EPA has had tremendous success: the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act frameworks that cut smog and helped rescue rivers like the Cuyahoga, which literally caught fire before EPA existed; the phase-out of leaded gasoline, linked to major drops in childhood lead exposure; and the near-elimination of DDT, which helped bring bald eagles back from the brink. It’s also served as a model for similar agencies around the world.

But all of that is under threat today, with the EPA being gutted by the current administration. Remember, the EPA was never created by its own act of Congress. It exists because Nixon reorganised the executive branch, which is part of why it's so vulnerable. That legacy is now under direct pressure. Since early 2025, the EPA has lost thousands of staff, with workforce levels at their lowest since the 1980s, while the administration has repeatedly cut the agency's budget, cancelled billions in already-authorized grants for clean air, water, and climate resilience, and repealed the 2009 endangerment finding underpinning US climate regulation. These actions represent the largest rollback of climate policy in U.S. history.

It's important to note, though, this isn’t the first time the EPA’s faced massive hurdles. Under Reagan, Ruckelshaus was brought back to lead the EPA because his predecessor, Anne Gorsuch (yes, mother of Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch) had almost entirely depleted the EPA by asking Congress to cut the agency's budget and halt enforcement activities.

So, what can you do? First, understand this isn’t some boring administrative issue. It directly impacts your health and that of your loved ones. Know where your reps stand on appropriations to the EPA and what they’re doing to support it. Make sure to give love to state and local environmental agencies, too. 

The Agency rose from the ashes before. With your help, it can do so once again.
